criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking water service pricing and affordability across the 500 largest community water systems in the United States.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines institutional ownership (public vs. private utilities) and state regulatory governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, utility ownership (investor-owned vs. government/cooperative) and state regulatory/cost-recovery rules (PUC rate regulation of public utilities, and pro-private rate/cost-recovery rules in NJ and PA such as Distribution System Improvement Charges [DSIC] and fair market value legislation) are explicitly listed rule-type mechanisms ('tariff or cost-recovery rules' and 'utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access') that directly govern household water tariffs and low-income service affordability.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical evidence: cross-sectional OLS regression analysis of N = 500 US community water systems combining compiled 2015 utility rate schedules with US EPA SDWIS, American Community Survey (2011-2015), PUC regulatory data, and US Drought Monitor data.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports two affordability/pricing outcomes relevant to household drinking water access: (1) typical household annual water bill ($ for 60,000 gallons/year) and (2) water affordability measured as the percentage of household income spent on water services by the lowest quintile of household income.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (500 largest US community water systems serving ~140 million residents, matched to city/county socioeconomic data), exposures (private vs. public ownership; state PUC regulation of public systems; pro-private state regulatory environment in NJ and PA), outcomes (annual household water bill and lowest-quintile income share spent on water), and study design (cross-sectional observational OLS regression) are all clearly specified, with regression coefficients and standard deviations/standardized coefficients reported.

evidence_quotes.quote: We examined the 500 largest community water systems in the US to explore whether ownership is related to annual water bills, and the percent of income that low-income households spend on water.
Our primary interest is in the difference in price and affordability by public and private water systems. We created a dummy variable to measure if the water system is owned by a private company.

To capture states which have created regulatory policy more favorable to private operators, we created a dummy variable to control for NJ and PA. PA and NJ are leaders in implementing new regulations that favor private operators (e.g. DSIC and fair market value)
We ran ordinary least squares regression models on factors related to water price and affordability controlling for ownership, regulation, water supply and community characteristics.
We measure water affordability as the percent of household income spent on water by the lowest quintile of household income

raw_response.exposure: Utility ownership structure (private investor-owned vs. public government or cooperative ownership) and state regulatory structure (state Public Utility Commission regulation of public water utilities; state pro-private regulatory/cost-recovery rules in NJ and PA such as Distribution System Improvement Charges and fair market value legislation)
raw_response.outcome: Household drinking water price (typical annual water bill in USD for 60,000 gallons/year in 2015) and water affordability (percent of household income spent on water services by the lowest quintile of household income)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 500 largest community water systems in the United States across 48 states and the District of Columbia (321 government-owned, 121 cooperative, 58 investor-owned), collectively serving approximately 140 million people in 2015 (unit of analysis: community water system matched to city/county population)
raw_response.rationale: This empirical cross-sectional study analyzes all 500 largest US community water systems using OLS regression to test how utility ownership (private investor-owned vs. public) and state regulatory structure (PUC regulation of public utilities and pro-private rate/cost-recovery rules such as DSIC surcharges and fair market value legislation in NJ and PA) affect annual household drinking water bills and water affordability for lowest-income-quintile households. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (utility ownership, regulatory structure, and tariff/cost-recovery rules directly governing household water affordability).
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional observational quantitative study (OLS regression analysis)
